items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that a topological ordering (TO, or topological sort) of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a linear ordering of its vertices such that for every directed edge [MATH: u \to v] from vertex [MATH: u] to vertex [MATH: v], [MATH: u] appears before [MATH: v] in the ordering.

Content:
We can find a topological ordering of a DAG using Kahn's algorithm.

Content:
Kahn's algorithm for topological ordering consists of two main steps:

Content:
- Step 1: Add all vertices with no incoming edges (where the indegree [MATH: \deg^-(v)=0]) to the TO, in any order.
- Step 2: Remove all vertices added in Step 1 from the graph, along with all their outgoing edges.

Content:
We repeat steps 1 and 2 until no vertices remain in the graph.

Content:
If, at any point, there are vertices remaining in the graph, but none have an in-degree of 0, it means the initial graph was not a directed acyclic graph (DAG). In this case, the remaining vertices form one or more cycles.

Content:
Thus, Kahn's algorithm can detect cycles effectively and identify the vertices involved! Cycle detection is an important problem in graph theory.

Content:
We can express Kahn's algorithm using pseudocode. Pseudocode is a simplified, programming language-independent way of describing an algorithm. It uses a mix of natural language and programming concepts, helping programmers to plan and visualize code logic without focusing on syntax.

Content:
The pseudocode for Kahn's algorithm is the following:

Content:
> Initialize the empty TO queue # topological ordering
>
> Initialize list V of all vertices in the graph
>
> Initialize list E of all edges in the graph
>
> while (V is not empty): # Until at least one vertex remains
>
> for (all v in V): # Go over all remaining vertices in V
>
> if (not (*,v) in E): # If the vertex v has no incoming edges
>
> Add v to TO queue
>
> Remove all outgoing edges for vertex v
>
> Remove v from V

Content:
Let's illustrate Kahn's algorithm by finding a topological ordering of the following DAG. Notice that the graph is disconnected, but this does not prevent Kahn's algorithm from producing a valid topological ordering (TO).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7325a852e9106317e8b9216a31c5fb0c]

Content:
We start with an empty TO: [MATH: \{\}.]

Content:
Step 1.1. Add all vertices with an indegree of [MATH: 0] to the TO; these vertices are [MATH: v_2, v_5, v_7,] and [MATH: v_{12}.] Since we can list them in any order, we will use ascending order based on their indices.
Hence, the TO is: [MATH: \{v_2, v_5, v_7,v_{12}\}.]

Content:
Step 2.1. Remove the vertices [MATH: v_2, v_5, v_7,] and [MATH: v_{12}] from the graph, along with all their outgoing edges. The resulting graph is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/226f37e021a1049a87457412a20a6963]

Content:
Step 2.1. Add all vertices with an indegree of [MATH: 0] to the TO; these vertices are [MATH: v_3, v_6, v_8,] and [MATH: v_{11}.]
Hence, the TO is: [MATH: \{v_2, v_5, v_7,v_{12}, v_3, v_6, v_8, v_{11}\}.]

Content:
Step 2.2. Remove the vertices [MATH: v_3, v_6, v_8,] and [MATH: v_{11}] from the graph, along with all their outgoing edges.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b8276e8142292a29be7090ad5685ba91]

Content:
Step 3.1. Add all vertices with an indegree of [MATH: 0] to the TO; these vertices are [MATH: v_1, v_4, v_9,] and [MATH: v_{10}.]
Hence, the TO is: [MATH: \{v_2, v_5, v_7,v_{12}, v_3, v_6, v_8, v_{11}, v_1, v_4, v_9, v_{10}\}.]

Content:
Step 3.2. No vertices remain; therefore, the topological ordering (TO) is complete, as shown in the image below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8b8f1609265da50843256bc3f43c48fa]

Content:
Notice that:

Content:
- At each step of the algorithm, we'll always add vertices to the topological ordering in ascending order of their indices for simplicity, but the vertices can be added in any order.
- Kahn's algorithm produces only one variant of a topological ordering (TO). In general, a TO is not unique, and finding all possible topological orderings requires other exhaustive search algorithms.

Recall that Kahn's algorithm for topological ordering (TO) consists of two main substeps:

  • Substep 1. Add all vertices with no incoming edges to the TO, in any order.

  • Substep 2. Remove all vertices processed in substep 1 from the graph and all the corresponding outgoing edges.

Repeat substeps 1 and 2 until no vertices remain in the graph.

The pseudocode for Kahn's algorithm is the following:

Initialize the empty queue TO # topological ordering

Initialize list V of all vertices in the graph

Initialize list E of all edges in the graph

while (V is not empty): # Until at least one vertex remains

for (all v in V): # Go over all remaining vertices in V

if (not (*,v) in E): # If the vertex v has no incoming edges

Add v to TO queue

Remove all outgoing edges for vertex v

Remove v from V

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that a topological ordering (TO, or topological sort) of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a linear ordering of its vertices such that for every directed edge [MATH: u \to v] from vertex [MATH: u] to vertex [MATH: v], [MATH: u] appears before [MATH: v] in the ordering.

Content:
We can find a topological ordering of a DAG using Kahn's algorithm.

Content:
Kahn's algorithm for topological ordering consists of two main steps:

Content:
- Step 1: Add all vertices with no incoming edges (where the indegree [MATH: \deg^-(v)=0]) to the TO, in any order.
- Step 2: Remove all vertices added in Step 1 from the graph, along with all their outgoing edges.

Content:
We repeat steps 1 and 2 until no vertices remain in the graph.

Content:
If, at any point, there are vertices remaining in the graph, but none have an in-degree of 0, it means the initial graph was not a directed acyclic graph (DAG). In this case, the remaining vertices form one or more cycles.

Content:
Thus, Kahn's algorithm can detect cycles effectively and identify the vertices involved! Cycle detection is an important problem in graph theory.

Content:
We can express Kahn's algorithm using pseudocode. Pseudocode is a simplified, programming language-independent way of describing an algorithm. It uses a mix of natural language and programming concepts, helping programmers to plan and visualize code logic without focusing on syntax.

Content:
The pseudocode for Kahn's algorithm is the following:

Content:
> Initialize the empty TO queue # topological ordering
>
> Initialize list V of all vertices in the graph
>
> Initialize list E of all edges in the graph
>
> while (V is not empty): # Until at least one vertex remains
>
> for (all v in V): # Go over all remaining vertices in V
>
> if (not (*,v) in E): # If the vertex v has no incoming edges
>
> Add v to TO queue
>
> Remove all outgoing edges for vertex v
>
> Remove v from V

Content:
Let's illustrate Kahn's algorithm by finding a topological ordering of the following DAG. Notice that the graph is disconnected, but this does not prevent Kahn's algorithm from producing a valid topological ordering (TO).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7325a852e9106317e8b9216a31c5fb0c]

Content:
We start with an empty TO: [MATH: \{\}.]

Content:
Step 1.1. Add all vertices with an indegree of [MATH: 0] to the TO; these vertices are [MATH: v_2, v_5, v_7,] and [MATH: v_{12}.] Since we can list them in any order, we will use ascending order based on their indices.
Hence, the TO is: [MATH: \{v_2, v_5, v_7,v_{12}\}.]

Content:
Step 2.1. Remove the vertices [MATH: v_2, v_5, v_7,] and [MATH: v_{12}] from the graph, along with all their outgoing edges. The resulting graph is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/226f37e021a1049a87457412a20a6963]

Content:
Step 2.1. Add all vertices with an indegree of [MATH: 0] to the TO; these vertices are [MATH: v_3, v_6, v_8,] and [MATH: v_{11}.]
Hence, the TO is: [MATH: \{v_2, v_5, v_7,v_{12}, v_3, v_6, v_8, v_{11}\}.]

Content:
Step 2.2. Remove the vertices [MATH: v_3, v_6, v_8,] and [MATH: v_{11}] from the graph, along with all their outgoing edges.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b8276e8142292a29be7090ad5685ba91]

Content:
Step 3.1. Add all vertices with an indegree of [MATH: 0] to the TO; these vertices are [MATH: v_1, v_4, v_9,] and [MATH: v_{10}.]
Hence, the TO is: [MATH: \{v_2, v_5, v_7,v_{12}, v_3, v_6, v_8, v_{11}, v_1, v_4, v_9, v_{10}\}.]

Content:
Step 3.2. No vertices remain; therefore, the topological ordering (TO) is complete, as shown in the image below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8b8f1609265da50843256bc3f43c48fa]

Content:
Notice that:

Content:
- At each step of the algorithm, we'll always add vertices to the topological ordering in ascending order of their indices for simplicity, but the vertices can be added in any order.
- Kahn's algorithm produces only one variant of a topological ordering (TO). In general, a TO is not unique, and finding all possible topological orderings requires other exhaustive search algorithms.

---

Item 2 — Example: Implementing One Iteration of Kahn's Algorithm

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that Kahn's algorithm for topological ordering consists of two main substeps:

- Substep 1. Add all vertices with no incoming edges to the TO, in any order.
- Substep 2. Remove all vertices processed in substep 1 from the graph and all the corresponding outgoing edges.

Repeat substeps 1 and 2 until no vertices remain in the graph.

In the given graph, only three vertices have no incoming edges. Hence, only these three should be added to the TO in substep 1 and then removed along with their outgoing edges in substep 2, completing the first iteration of the algorithm.

These three vertices and their outgoing edges are highlighted in the image below.

[IMG: /graphics/f44413b2ffddd177a53caef591ff1603]

Therefore, the graph after the first iteration of the algorithm will be as follows:

[IMG: /graphics/9f6618eb49f371fa8cd2e7a3a5a73551]

So, the correct answer is graph [MATH: \textrm{II}.]
